title: AI use rises in PH amid Asean push, Pax Silica protests
summary: MANILA, Philippines — The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) among Filipinos of working age has increased, but the Philippines continues to trail three Southeast Asian economies even as…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) among Filipinos of working age has increased, but the Philippines continues to trail three Southeast Asian economies even as Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) member states push for wider adoption of the technology among businesses.

About 20.7% of Filipinos aged 15 to 64 used generative AI products in the second quarter of 2026, above the global average of 18.8%, according to the Microsoft AI Economy Institute’s Global AI Diffusion Q2 2026 Trends and Insights report.

In his analysis of the findings, University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman associate professor and Inquirer data scientist Dr. Rogelio Alicor Panao said the country’s adoption rate had increased from 17.1% in the first half of 2025, a gain of 3.6 percentage points. The Philippines ranked 56th among 147 economies assessed.
“At first glance, the 3.6-percentage-point increase looks encouraging,” Panao wrote.

But the regional comparison shows that the country still has ground to cover. The Philippines ranked fourth among nine Southeast Asian economies included in the report, behind Singapore, which recorded 64.3% usage; Vietnam, 27.9%; and Malaysia, 22.6%.
Across Asia, the Philippines also trailed South Korea, at 40.6%; Taiwan, at 33.8%; and Japan, at 24.7%. It remained ahead of India, at 18.5%, and China, at 17.5%.
“In other words, the Philippines is making progress, but it is hardly at the forefront of regional AI adoption,” Panao said.

Microsoft’s AI diffusion measure represents the share of the working-age population, or those aged 15 to 64, who used a generative AI product during the reporting period. It is based on aggregated and anonymized usage data adjusted for differences in operating systems, device markets, internet access and population.

The figure measures individual use of generative AI products. It does not establish how many Filipino companies have integrated AI into their operations or whether individuals use the tools primarily for work or personal purposes.
Asean leaders push AI adoption among MSMEs
The findings come as the Philippines uses its Asean chairship to advance regional cooperation on digital technology and artificial intelligence.

During the 49th Asean Summit in Manila, regional leaders adopted the Asean Leaders’ Declaration on AI-Powered Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME) Growth, committing member states to expanding smaller businesses’ access to AI tools and making the technology more practical and affordable.

The declaration outlines 12 commitments, including promoting AI literacy among entrepreneurs, helping businesses assess their readiness to use the technology and improving access for underserved enterprises, particularly women-led businesses and those in rural and remote communities.
It also encourages partnerships among governments, startups, technology companies, universities and research institutions to develop affordable AI solutions for MSMEs.
Member states also recognized the need for safeguards, including cybersecurity, personal data protection, transparency, accountability, human oversight and respect for intellectual property rights.

Separately, Asean leaders signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which seeks to establish common rules and cooperation mechanisms for digital trade, cross-border e-commerce, electronic payments and emerging technologies, including AI.

The agreement still needs to undergo national ratification processes before implementation. Trade Secretary Ma. Cristina Roque said Asean was targeting its rollout under Singapore’s chairship in 2027.
“We expect, or hope, that Singapore will implement it during its chairship next year, in 2027,” Roque said during a briefing at the summit.
Pax Silica draws public opposition
The government’s push for AI-related industries has also faced public scrutiny, particularly over the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative and a proposed industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

Pax Silica seeks to strengthen international supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy, logistics and AI infrastructure. The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with the government identifying a proposed 1,620-hectare economic zone in New Clark City as a local industrial hub under the partnership.

The proposed development has drawn criticism from environmental organizations, Indigenous groups and other civil society organizations concerned about possible community displacement, land use, water consumption, electricity requirements and environmental effects.

The Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), which is overseeing the proposed development, has described it as a manufacturing-driven industrial ecosystem rather than a large data center complex.

It has also said it was updating the socioeconomic profiles of families and Indigenous peoples in areas that could be affected, in coordination with the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, to identify appropriate safeguards and assistance.

The controversy was visible during the opening of the Asean Summit on Nov. 15, following the arrest of more than 300 protesters in Manila and Muntinlupa as groups prepared to march toward the summit venue.
The demonstrations involved several issues, including opposition to the proposed Pax Silica hub, the anticipated visit of U.S. President Donald Trump and labor-related concerns.
Economic conditions pose wider challenges
In his analysis, Panao also examined the country’s AI adoption against its economic outlook and ability to attract investments in technology-related industries.

The Asian Development Bank’s September 2026 outlook lowered its Philippine economic growth forecast for 2026 to 3.3%, from 3.8% in its July projection. Its 2027 forecast was also reduced to 5.1%, from 5.3%.
The ADB cited weaker investment during the first half of the year and higher prices of imported fuel and other essential commodities among the factors weighing on growth.

“While Vietnam, Indonesia, and Malaysia attract electronics and technology investments linked to AI supply chains, the Philippines continues to struggle with weak infrastructure spending and sluggish consumption,” Panao said.
For Panao, the country’s increasing use of generative AI must be considered alongside its capacity to attract technology investments and build the economic conditions needed to support the industry.
“The Philippines wants ASEAN to move faster on AI. Yet its own adoption figures and investment outlook suggest that it has considerable catching up to do,” he said.
“Perhaps the bigger challenge is not putting AI on the regional agenda, but making sure the country is not left behind as that agenda takes shape,” he added.
